name: Etruscan
confidence_why: Bonfante and Bonfante 2002 and Skutsch 1907 both put a heavy stress on the first syllable, inferred from the vowel syncope of inscriptions after about 500 BCE, and Belfiore 2020 concurs that the earlier free accent had become a stress accent by the early fifth century; the only qualifications are that archaic Etruscan had a different accent and that a few Greek names keep their Greek accent position.

new_statements.quote: The second Etruscan innovation is the intensive initial accent which also spread in Latin and the Italic languages, and which produced a larger number of syncopated words in Etruscan than in Latin. [...] Around 500 the evidence of the inscriptions shows that a change took place in the way both Etruscan and Latin were pronounced, when the so-called initial stress accent came into Etruscan and Latin (as well as other languages of Italy). At this time all words were heavily stressed, or accented, on the first syllable. The rest of the word was proportionately less stressed, and vowels dropped out ('syncope'), or were replaced by 'weaker' vowels, less strongly pronounced.

new_statements.rule_in_words: From about 500 BCE every Etruscan word carried a strong (intensive/expiratory) stress on its first syllable; later syllables were weakly stressed and their vowels weakened or dropped (syncope: praesentes > presnts, Ramutha > Ramtha, Rasenna > Rasna, Menerva > Menrva, Alexandros > Alcsentre; final vowels also lost, suthithi > suthith).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the statement is dated (the initial stress accent 'came into' Etruscan around 500 BCE), so it describes the language from the late archaic period onward, not the earliest inscriptions.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern Etruscan as written in Italy (Neo-Etruscan / post-500 BCE for the initial-stress claims); Belfiore 2020 distinguishes an archaic phase (7th-6th c. BCE) with a melodic/free accent from the later stress-accent phase. Eichner 2012/2013 (held by the project, silent on accent position) concern the Lemnos stele, a Tyrsenian relative, not Etruscan proper. No dialectal (northern vs southern Etruscan) statement about stress was found.

new_statements.translation: γ) Syncope of internal syllables through the effect of an expiratory accent standing on the first syllable: aϑrpa Atropos, atlenta Atalanta, aχle Achilles, caśntra Cassandra, clutmsta Klytaimestra, elχsntre, elsntre beside elaχsantre Alexandros, hercle Herakles beside heracle, menle Menelaos, menrva Menerva, pecse Pegasos, pultuke beside pulutuke Polydeukes etc. [col. 788] In a curious contrast to the rule stand forms such as plunice (?) Polyneikes, mliϑuns Meliton (?), mnele Menelaos, tlamunus Telamonios, of which at least the last hardly admits doubt, but whose sound shape seems to presuppose an accent position corresponding to the Greek one.

new_statements.rule_in_words: An expiratory (stress) accent on the first syllable, inferred from the syncope of internal syllables in Etruscan renderings of Greek names; a counter-tendency of anaptyxis (svarabhakti vowels, 'schwa etruscum') in the syllables weakened by the accent (point δ).
new_statements.exceptions: A few Greek loans (plunice, mliϑuns, mnele, tlamunus) show a syncope pattern that presupposes the Greek accent position rather than initial stress.

new_statements.quote: Anche i fenomeni legati al cambio di accento sembrano procedere di pari passo: se il passaggio da melodico/ libero a tonico sembra ancora in corso nel V sec. questo limite va però spostato agli inizi del secolo, come ben dimostra il caso di avile/ avele/ avale, che accanto ad un ben testimoniato avile(s) di VII e VI sec. (22 attestazioni ex ThLE, 27 ex ET), mostra un buon numero di attestazioni della forma avele(s) nel VI sec. (12 ex ThLE; 18 ex ET), e un'unica forma avale della prima metà del V sec. (ET Cr 3.23). Lo studio recente di Rigobianco (2017) richiama inoltre ulteriori aspetti morfotattici legati alla presenza di un accento secondario in età arcaica.
new_statements.translation: The phenomena tied to the change of accent also seem to proceed in step: if the shift from a melodic/free accent to a stress (tonic) accent still seems to be in progress in the 5th century, this limit must however be moved to the beginning of that century, as the case of avile/avele/avale shows well, which beside a well-attested avile(s) of the 7th and 6th centuries (22 attestations in ThLE, 27 in ET) shows a good number of attestations of the form avele(s) in the 6th century (12 in ThLE; 18 in ET), and a single form avale of the first half of the 5th century (ET Cr 3.23). The recent study by Rigobianco (2017) moreover recalls further morphotactic aspects linked to the presence of a secondary accent in the archaic period.

new_statements.quote: The loss of vowels in Etruscan spelling after the first syllable, resulting in clusters of consonants, was due to an intensive stress accent which around 500 Bc affected Etruscan as well as other languages of Italy (Latin, Umbrian, Oscan, Sabellian). The first syllable was heavily accented, with the result that following vowels weakened (a > e > i), and eventually dropped out. This abbreviation, or syncope, is most obvious in the later, neo-Etruscan inscriptions of the fourth century Bc and the Hellenistic period. On Etruscan mirrors, for example, we find the Greek name Alexandros written in the abbreviated form Alcsentre, and even Elcsntre.

new_statements.rule_in_words: From about 500 BC Etruscan had a strong (intensive) stress accent on the first syllable of the word; post-initial vowels weakened (a > e > i) and were then lost (syncope), visible above all in neo-Etruscan (4th c. BC and later) spellings such as Alcsentre/Elcsntre, Ramtha, Rasna, Clutmsta, turce.
new_statements.exceptions: No exceptions to initial stress are stated. The text adds the converse tendency of anaptyxis in internal syllables (Aritimi, Herecele, Menerva) and notes that the syncope belongs to the later period (the Archaic, pre-500 BC inscriptions are unsyncopated), i.e. the initial accent is dated to c. 500 BC onward.
new_statements.identity_note: Etruscan of the inscriptions (7th-1st c. BC); the initial stress accent is dated by Bonfante to c. 500 BC onward (its effects visible in neo-Etruscan spellings of the 4th c. BC and later), the Archaic inscriptions being unsyncopated; no dialect/regional distinction is made for the accent.

readall_conflicts: No source contradicts the catalog's fixed: initial syllable placement. Two qualifications, both diachronic rather than contradictory: (1) Bonfante & Bonfante 2002 (p. 80-81) and Belfiore 2020 (p. 239) both date the arrival of the strong initial stress accent to around 500 BCE / the early 5th century, and Belfiore describes the earlier archaic accent as 'melodico/libero' (melodic, free), so the fixed: initial syllable rule is stated for Etruscan from the late archaic period onward, not for the 7th-6th-century inscriptions; (2) Skutsch 1907 (col. 788) notes a handful of Greek names (plunice, mnele, tlamunus) whose syncope pattern presupposes the Greek accent position instead of initial stress. Neither of the two listed works (Wallace 2008, Bonfante 1990) could be opened, so nothing from them is on record.

sources.quote: These vowel weakenings and syncopes, found in Etruscan, Latin, and the Sabellic languages, are usually explained as being due to the adoption of an initial stress accent. This was certainly not inherited by the Italic languages, since Proto-Indo-European had a free pitch accent. Latin shows no signs of weakening in the earliest inscriptions, and so may not have yet developed the initial accent; we cannot be sure whether it was borrowed from Etruscan, or whether it was a new development there as well.
